title: Is backtesting really works?
author: cryptign
selftext: Hey guys, is backtesting really works? Also who any ai tool indicator or strategy that really has high winning percentage? Looking forward to something will guide me. Ty

comments.author: HelloBello30
comments.body:
normally i cringe when people say "oh my sweet summer child", but i can't think of a more appropriate line here.

To answer your question.. yes backtesting is useful.. and yes there are high winning percentage strategies out there, such as ones that involve holding unrealized losses for longer periods of times, but high winning doesn't mean that you will make profit.

replies.author: HelloBello30
replies.body:
A couple of ways. In general the wins are more frequent but smaller than the losses. Say you have 10 trades. You win $1 on 8 of them. But then you lose $5 on each of the two losses. Thats an 80% win rate but you lost money.

Win rate is also sort of deceptive depending on what you count. IE some strategies claim 99% win rates, but they're basically not counting positions that are under water because they haven't formally exited/closed them. IF they bounce back, they will count towards a win. That's a big slow "if" that locks up capital and ruins opportunity.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Backtesting works as a filter for bad ideas, but it can't prove that a good-looking result will hold, because the best-looking test is often just the luckiest one out of many tries. A high win rate also isn't the goal, since a strategy can win 90% of its trades and still lose money if the losses are bigger than the wins. I'd be careful with any tool promising a high win rate, and judge things by profit per trade after fees, tested on data the rule never saw. Then run it small in paper mode before real money. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to test a rule against history with fees included.

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body:
Backtesting is useful when the rule is fixed first and the test can expose a failure: wrong signal timing, costs eating the result, or drawdown that the account cannot survive. A high winning percentage can still lose money if the occasional loss is much larger. Keep open losses in the equity curve and validate on later data rather than repeatedly tuning the same period.

comments.author: pulllab
comments.body: It helps, but only as a filter, not as proof. A backtest can tell you an idea is broken, or that it only worked because you kept tweaking it until it fit the past. What I look for before taking anything seriously is a fixed rule written down first, realistic costs and slippage included, and a test on data the rule was not tuned on. A high win rate on its own does not mean much either — lots of small wins can still be wiped out by a few large losses.

comments.author: External-Revenue4978
comments.body: Backtesting is useful for finding out whether an idea has any evidence behind it, but it can't promise future performance. A high win rate can also be misleading if the occasional loser wipes out twenty small gains. I've looked at shorter directional opportunities on Moon and I'd rather see a simple strategy tested on unseen data with realistic costs than trust an AI indicator claiming near perfect accuracy.
